# Payables and Vendors {#sec-payables}

A State Directorate of Health Services buys paper, toner, bulbs, cement, chairs and medicines for its eight district offices. Each office raises orders, receives the goods, accepts the bills and pays the vendors. Thousands of payments go out in a year. Most are routine. A few are not. A vendor's bank account is changed for twelve days, just long enough for one large payment. A firm is registered on a Monday and paid on the following Monday. One office pays almost 40% more than its neighbours for the same toner cartridge, month after month. None of this shows in a payment register read line by line.

Payables are where an organisation's money leaves it. So they attract both error and fraud. Earlier chapters of this book already hold many tests that apply here. They find duplicate invoices, bills split below a limit, look-alike vendor names and links between employees and vendors. This chapter brings those tests together for one department's payables, in a few lines each. It then adds the classic payables tests that the book has not yet covered. These are a review of the vendor master and its change log, and the **three-way match** of order, receipt and invoice. They also include **price benchmarking** of the same item across offices and months. Finally it combines the flags into a view of each vendor, and follows two cases to the end.

As in every chapter of this part, a flag is not a finding. Most flagged items will have a good reason. The aim is to find the few that need a question.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## The purchase-to-pay cycle {#sec-pay-cycle}

Every purchase passes through the same steps. Auditors call them the **purchase-to-pay cycle**. Each step leaves a record, and each record can be checked against the others.

| Step | Record | What can go wrong |
|------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------|
| 1. A vendor is registered | Vendor master, and its change log | Fictitious vendors, duplicate vendors, bank details changed to divert a payment |
| 2. The office orders the goods | Purchase order | Buying without an order, or at an inflated rate |
| 3. The goods arrive | Goods receipt | Short or no delivery |
| 4. The vendor sends a bill | Invoice | Billing more than was delivered, or above the agreed rate, or twice |
| 5. The office pays | Payment | Paying before delivery, paying the wrong account, paying twice |

: The purchase-to-pay cycle {#tbl-pay-cycle}

The flow is simple. Vendor, then order, then receipt, then invoice, then payment. The controls are simple too. Nobody should be paid unless the vendor is genuine, the goods were ordered, the goods arrived, and the bill matches both. The tests in this chapter check each of these, for every transaction.

## Our data, the payables of a State health directorate {#sec-pay-data}

Our auditee is an imaginary Directorate of Health Services of a State, with eight district offices. We have its purchase and payment records for 2024-25. All names, firms and numbers are made up. There are nine tables.

- `vendors` is the vendor master. Each vendor has an id, a name, a PAN, a GSTIN, a bank account, an address and the date it was registered.
- `vendor_changes` is the change log of the vendor master. It records each change of bank account, with the old and new values, the date and the user who made it.
- `employees` is the employee master, with each employee's office, designation, PAN, bank account and address.
- `purchase_orders` has one row for each order. To keep the example simple, each order is for one item, with a quantity and a rate. With several lines in an order, the same joins work on the order number and the line number.
- `receipts` has one row for each delivery. `challan_date` is the date on the vendor's delivery challan, when the goods arrived. `grn_date` is the date the store entered the goods receipt note in the system. Some orders arrive in two deliveries.
- `invoices` has one row for each bill, with the order it refers to, the quantity, the rate and the amount. Rates include tax.
- `payments` has one row for each payment, with the bank account it was paid into. Bills are paid in full, without deductions, to keep the example simple.
- `past_paid` holds the total paid to each vendor in each of the three earlier years, from the old accounting system.
- `rate_contract` holds the State rate contract for cement, and `bank_totals` the monthly total of payments in the department's bank statement.

Most of the data is routine. Offices buy from two or three regular vendors for each item. Prices differ a little by office, since remote offices pay more for transport. Large orders get a better rate, and prices rise slowly through the year. Some vendors changed their bank accounts for good reasons. Some goods receipts were entered in the system a few days late. Into this, these cases have been planted.

1. **A bank account changed around a large payment.** Narmada Office Solutions, a regular supplier of paper, has its account changed three days before a large payment, and changed back nine days after it.
2. **A vendor paid within a week of registration.** Trinetra Medical Agencies is registered, given an order, and paid within seven days. It has no GSTIN, and it is paid large sums over the following months.
3. **A dormant vendor wakes up.** Gomti Furniture House was last paid three years ago. In February 2025 it receives large orders of chairs.
4. **A duplicate vendor.** Maa Durga Medical Agency is registered with the same PAN as Maa Durga Medical Agencies, a slightly different name, and a different bank account.
5. **A vendor sharing a bank account with an employee.** Sagar Lighting House is paid into the account of an employee of the Madhopur office.
6. **A GSTIN that fails its check.** One character of the GSTIN of Pragati Paper Mart is wrong.
7. **Breaks in the three-way match.** Invoices with no order, invoices dated before the order, more billed than received, rates billed above the order, payments made before the goods arrived, and orders received in part but paid in full.
8. **One office paying more.** The Dhanpur office buys toner cartridges from one vendor at about 40% above what other offices pay.

There are a few more, which the tests of earlier chapters will find. Let us build the data.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the payables data"
set.seed(2425)

offices <- c("Rampur", "Keshavnagar", "Sitapur", "Bhawanipur", "Chandgarh", "Dhanpur",
             "Madhopur", "Ratanpur")
# Remote offices pay a little more, for transport
office_factor <- c(Rampur = 1, Keshavnagar = 1.02, Sitapur = 1.04, Bhawanipur = 1,
                   Chandgarh = 1.06, Dhanpur = 1.03, Madhopur = 1.05, Ratanpur = 1.08)

items <- tribble(
  ~item,                ~unit,          ~base_rate, ~qty_mean, ~trade,
  "A4 paper",           "ream",         265,        150,       "Stationery",
  "Toner cartridge",    "piece",        3400,       12,        "Stationery",
  "LED bulb 9W",        "piece",        96,         300,       "Electrical",
  "Cement bag",         "bag of 50 kg", 380,        250,       "Building",
  "Office chair",       "piece",        5200,       10,        "Furniture",
  "Paracetamol 500 mg", "strip of 10",  18,         4000,      "Medical",
  "Surgical gloves",    "box of 100",   420,        80,        "Medical"
)

# ---- Vendor master ----
first <- c("Shri Ganesh", "Shiv Shakti", "Kaveri", "Vindhya", "Sai Krupa", "Jai Ambe", "Navin",
           "Pragati", "Unnati", "Sagar", "Himalaya", "Gomti", "Ashoka", "Kamal", "Suraj", "Chandan",
           "Ganga", "Yamuna", "Satpura", "Aravali", "Nilgiri", "Saraswati", "Lakshmi", "Prakash",
           "Deep", "Jyoti", "Anand", "Mangal", "Shubham", "Vardhman", "Krishna", "Gopal", "Mahavir",
           "Nandan", "Kirti", "Sunrise", "Evergreen", "Pioneer", "Supreme", "Royal", "Classic",
           "Modern", "National", "City", "Star", "Diamond", "Golden", "Silver", "Tirupati", "Om")
suffix <- list(Stationery = c("Stationers", "Paper Mart", "Office Supplies", "Computer Supplies"),
               Electrical = c("Electricals", "Electric Stores", "Lighting House"),
               Building   = c("Cement Depot", "Building Materials", "Hardware Stores"),
               Furniture  = c("Furniture House", "Furnishers", "Steel Furniture"),
               Medical    = c("Medical Agencies", "Pharma Distributors", "Surgicals", "Medicos"))
trade_mix <- c(Stationery = 50, Electrical = 30, Building = 30, Furniture = 25, Medical = 45)
v_trade <- rep(names(trade_mix), trade_mix)
v_name <- character(length(v_trade))
taken <- c("Gomti Furniture House", "Kaveri Electricals", "Sagar Lighting House", "Pragati Paper Mart",
           "Unnati Computer Supplies", "Jai Ambe Cement Depot", "Shiv Shakti Steel Furniture")
for (i in seq_along(v_trade)) {
  repeat {
    nm <- paste(sample(first, 1), sample(suffix[[v_trade[i]]], 1))
    if (!nm %in% c(v_name, taken)) break
  }
  v_name[i] <- nm
}
towns <- c(offices, "Rajdhani Nagar")
markets <- c("Gandhi Market", "Station Road", "Sadar Bazar", "Civil Lines", "Nehru Chowk",
             "Industrial Area", "Main Road", "Subhash Marg", "Tilak Nagar", "Kotwali Road")
gst_chars <- c(0:9, LETTERS)
gstin_check_char <- function(first14) {
  v <- match(strsplit(first14, "")[[1]], gst_chars) - 1
  p <- v * rep(c(1, 2), 7)
  total <- sum(p %/% 36 + p %% 36)
  gst_chars[((36 - total %% 36) %% 36) + 1]
}
make_pan <- function(name, holder) {
  paste0(paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = ""), holder, substr(name, 1, 1),
         sprintf("%04d", sample(1000:9999, 1)), sample(LETTERS, 1))
}
make_gstin <- function(pan, entity = "1") {
  f14 <- paste0("22", pan, entity, "Z")
  paste0(f14, gstin_check_char(f14))
}
make_acct <- function(n) paste0(sample(c("3104", "5021", "6620", "1187"), n, TRUE),
                                sprintf("%08d", sample(1e7:99999999, n)))
make_addr <- function(n, prefix = "Shop No.") paste0(prefix, " ", sample(1:120, n, TRUE), ", ",
                                                     sample(markets, n, TRUE), ", ",
                                                     sample(towns, n, TRUE, prob = c(rep(1, 8), 3)))

nv <- length(v_name)
holder <- sample(c("C", "F", "P"), nv, TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.45, 0.30))
vendors <- tibble(
  key = seq_len(nv), vendor_name = v_name, trade = v_trade,
  pan = map2_chr(v_name, holder, make_pan),
  bank_account = make_acct(nv),
  address = expand_grid(no = 1:150, m = markets, t = towns) |>
    mutate(a = paste0("Shop No. ", no, ", ", m, ", ", t)) |>
    filter(!no %in% c(2, 5, 7, 9, 14, 18, 27, 33, 45, 61, 80)) |>
    slice_sample(n = nv) |> pull(a),
  created_on = as.Date("2014-04-01") + sample(0:3500, nv, TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(gstin = map_chr(pan, make_gstin))
# A few vendors registered in the year
new_keys <- sample(which(vendors$trade != "Furniture"), 11)
vendors$created_on[new_keys] <- as.Date("2024-04-15") + sample(0:240, 11)

# ---- Planted vendors (added to the master) ----
pv <- tribble(
  ~vendor_name,                  ~trade,       ~holder, ~address,                                  ~created_on,
  "Narmada Office Solutions",    "Stationery", "F",     "Plot 14, Industrial Area, Rajdhani Nagar", "2016-05-10",
  "Trinetra Medical Agencies",   "Medical",    "P",     "House No. 61, Tilak Nagar, Ratanpur",      "2024-11-04",
  "Vindhya Health Distributors", "Medical",    "F",     "Shop No. 9, Sadar Bazar, Keshavnagar",     "2024-08-12",
  "Gomti Furniture House",       "Furniture",  "F",     "Shop No. 33, Main Road, Bhawanipur",       "2015-09-21",
  "Maa Durga Medical Agencies",  "Medical",    "F",     "Shop No. 7, Station Road, Sitapur",        "2017-02-14",
  "Maa Durga Medical Agency",    "Medical",    "F",     "Shop 7, Station Rd, Sitapur",              "2024-06-20",
  "Kaveri Electricals",          "Electrical", "C",     "Plot 3, Industrial Area, Rajdhani Nagar",  "2015-01-12",
  "Kaveri Electricals",          "Electrical", "C",     "Shop No. 18, Gandhi Market, Chandgarh",    "2021-07-05",
  "Sagar Lighting House",        "Electrical", "P",     "Shop No. 45, Nehru Chowk, Madhopur",       "2019-03-11",
  "Pragati Paper Mart",          "Stationery", "F",     "Shop No. 2, Kotwali Road, Rampur",         "2018-10-01",
  "Unnati Computer Supplies",    "Stationery", "F",     "Shop No. 27, Civil Lines, Dhanpur",        "2018-06-15",
  "Jai Ambe Cement Depot",       "Building",   "F",     "Shop No. 80, Main Road, Chandgarh",        "2016-12-01",
  "Shiv Shakti Steel Furniture", "Furniture",  "F",     "Shop No. 5, Subhash Marg, Madhopur",       "2017-08-08"
) |>
  mutate(key = nv + row_number(), created_on = as.Date(created_on),
         pan = map2_chr(vendor_name, holder, make_pan),
         bank_account = make_acct(n()))
pv$pan[6] <- pv$pan[5]                                     # same PAN, variant name
pv$pan[8] <- pv$pan[7]                                     # same PAN, second registration
pv$bank_account[8] <- pv$bank_account[7]
pv <- pv |> mutate(gstin = map2_chr(pan, c(rep("1", 7), "2", rep("1", 5)), make_gstin))
pv$gstin[2] <- NA                                          # new vendor, no GSTIN
g <- pv$gstin[10]                                          # one character typed wrongly
substr(g, 9, 9) <- if (substr(g, 9, 9) == "4") "7" else "4"
pv$gstin[10] <- g
vendors <- bind_rows(vendors, select(pv, -holder))
pk <- set_names(pv$key, c("bank", "newfast", "newok", "dormant", "durga", "durga2", "kaveri1",
                          "kaveri2", "sagar", "pragati", "unnati", "jaiambe", "shivshakti"))

# Vendor ids in a random order, so that planted vendors are not at the end
vendors <- vendors |>
  mutate(vendor_id = sprintf("V%03d", sample(101:(100 + n())))) |>
  arrange(vendor_id)
vid <- function(k) vendors$vendor_id[match(k, vendors$key)]

# ---- Employee master ----
fn <- c("Amit", "Sunita", "Rakesh", "Pooja", "Vijay", "Neha", "Suresh", "Kavita", "Manoj", "Rekha",
        "Deepak", "Anita", "Rajesh", "Meena", "Sanjay", "Priya", "Ashok", "Seema", "Ramesh", "Geeta")
ln <- c("Verma", "Sharma", "Yadav", "Singh", "Gupta", "Mishra", "Patel", "Tiwari", "Chauhan",
        "Pandey", "Jain", "Saxena", "Dubey", "Rawat", "Thakur")
ne <- 320
employees <- tibble(
  emp_id = sprintf("E%04d", sample(1001:1999, ne)),
  emp_name = paste(sample(fn, ne, TRUE), sample(ln, ne, TRUE)),
  office = sample(c(offices, "Directorate"), ne, TRUE),
  designation = sample(c("Clerk", "Senior Clerk", "Store keeper", "Accountant", "Pharmacist",
                         "Junior Engineer", "Medical Officer", "Staff Nurse", "Driver"), ne, TRUE),
  bank_account = make_acct(ne)
) |>
  mutate(pan = map_chr(emp_name, \(x) make_pan(word(x, 2), "P")),
         address = paste0("House No. ", sample(1:400, ne, TRUE), ", ",
                          sample(c("Shastri Colony", "Ram Nagar", "Vikas Puri", "Officers Colony",
                                   "Indira Nagar", "Ward No. 6"), ne, TRUE), ", ",
                          if_else(office == "Directorate", "Rajdhani Nagar", office))) |>
  arrange(emp_id)
# Planted. The vendor Sagar Lighting House is paid into an employee's account
emp_link <- which(employees$office == "Madhopur" & employees$designation != "Driver")[1]
employees$designation[emp_link] <- "Junior Engineer"
vendors$bank_account[vendors$key == pk["sagar"]] <- employees$bank_account[emp_link]

# ---- Purchase orders ----
fy_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-02-28"), by = "day")
work <- fy_days[!weekdays(fy_days) %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday")]
# each office buys each item from two or three regular vendors of the trade
regular <- vendors |> filter(!key %in% pv$key | key %in% pk[c("bank", "kaveri1", "pragati", "unnati",
                                                                  "jaiambe", "shivshakti", "durga", "sagar")])
supply <- expand_grid(office = offices, item = items$item) |>
  left_join(select(items, item, trade), by = "item") |>
  mutate(vkeys = map2(trade, office, \(t, o) {
    pool <- regular |> filter(trade == t, created_on < as.Date("2024-04-01") | key %in% vendors$key[vendors$key %in% new_keys])
    sample(pool$key, 3)
  }))
# Planted vendors that must be regular suppliers somewhere
fix_v <- function(o, it, k) supply$vkeys[[which(supply$office == o & supply$item == it)]][1] <<- k
fix_v("Rampur", "A4 paper", pk["bank"]); fix_v("Keshavnagar", "A4 paper", pk["bank"])
fix_v("Madhopur", "LED bulb 9W", pk["sagar"]); fix_v("Chandgarh", "LED bulb 9W", pk["kaveri1"])
fix_v("Rampur", "A4 paper", pk["pragati"]); supply$vkeys[[which(supply$office == "Rampur" & supply$item == "A4 paper")]][2] <- pk["bank"]
fix_v("Dhanpur", "Toner cartridge", pk["unnati"]); fix_v("Chandgarh", "Cement bag", pk["jaiambe"])
fix_v("Sitapur", "Surgical gloves", pk["durga"]); fix_v("Madhopur", "Office chair", pk["shivshakti"])

n_po <- 1050
po <- tibble(po_date = sort(sample(work, n_po, TRUE)),
             office = sample(offices, n_po, TRUE),
             item = sample(items$item, n_po, TRUE, prob = c(3, 2, 2, 1.5, 1, 2, 2))) |>
  left_join(items, by = "item") |>
  mutate(vkey = map2_int(office, item, \(o, it) {
           ks <- supply$vkeys[[which(supply$office == o & supply$item == it)]]
           sample(ks, 1, prob = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2))
         }),
         qty = pmax(round(qty_mean * rlnorm(n(), 0, 0.5)), 2),
         # bigger orders get a better price, and prices rise a little through the year
         qty_effect = case_when(qty > 1.8 * qty_mean ~ 0.95, qty < 0.5 * qty_mean ~ 1.06, .default = 1),
         trend = 1 + 0.05 * as.numeric(po_date - as.Date("2024-04-01")) / 365,
         rate = round(base_rate * office_factor[office] * qty_effect * trend * rnorm(n(), 1, 0.035), 2))
# A vendor registered during the year cannot get an order before it exists
early <- which(po$po_date < vendors$created_on[match(po$vkey, vendors$key)])
for (j in early) {
  ks <- supply$vkeys[[which(supply$office == po$office[j] & supply$item == po$item[j])]]
  ok <- ks[vendors$created_on[match(ks, vendors$key)] <= po$po_date[j]]
  po$vkey[j] <- if (length(ok) > 0) ok[1] else sample(regular$key[regular$trade == po$trade[j] &
                                                                    regular$created_on < as.Date("2024-04-01")], 1)
}
# Cement is on a State rate contract, with a lower rate from 1 October 2024
rate_contract <- tibble(item = "Cement bag", effective_from = as.Date(c("2024-04-01", "2024-10-01")),
                        contract_rate = c(380, 355))
po <- po |>
  mutate(rate = if_else(item == "Cement bag",
                        if_else(po_date < as.Date("2024-10-01"), 380, 355), rate))

# Planted. Dhanpur buys toner from Unnati Computer Supplies at about 40% above the usual price
idx <- which(po$office == "Dhanpur" & po$item == "Toner cartridge")
po$vkey[idx] <- pk["unnati"]
po$rate[idx] <- round(3400 * runif(length(idx), 1.40, 1.50) * po$trend[idx], 2)
# Planted. Chandgarh keeps ordering cement at the old contract rate after the rate was lowered
idx <- which(po$office == "Chandgarh" & po$item == "Cement bag" & po$po_date >= as.Date("2024-10-01"))
po$rate[idx[seq_len(min(3, length(idx)))]] <- 380

add_po <- function(d, o, it, k, q, r) {
  tibble(po_date = as.Date(d), office = o, item = it, vkey = k, qty = q, rate = r) |>
    left_join(items, by = "item")
}
extra <- bind_rows(
  # Planted. Four LED orders at Madhopur, each just below Rs 2.5 lakh, within nine days
  add_po(c("2024-12-02", "2024-12-04", "2024-12-09", "2024-12-11"), "Madhopur", "LED bulb 9W",
         pk["sagar"], c(2450, 2380, 2490, 2420), 99.5),
  # Planted. The new vendor, ordered from on the day after it was created, and later
  add_po(c("2024-11-05", "2024-11-25", "2024-12-16", "2025-01-13", "2025-02-03"), "Ratanpur",
         "Surgical gloves", pk["newfast"], c(900, 1400, 2000, 1800, 2000), c(452, 455, 455, 458, 460)),
  # The genuine new vendor, an urgent purchase during a fever outbreak
  add_po(c("2024-08-13", "2024-09-10", "2024-10-22"), "Keshavnagar", "Paracetamol 500 mg",
         pk["newok"], c(60000, 30000, 25000), c(17.9, 18.1, 18.2)),
  # Planted. A dormant vendor wakes up with large orders of chairs
  add_po(c("2025-02-10", "2025-02-24", "2025-03-05"), "Bhawanipur", "Office chair",
         pk["dormant"], c(160, 140, 120), c(5350, 5380, 5400)),
  # The variant Maa Durga vendor gets orders at Sitapur too
  add_po(c("2024-07-15", "2024-09-30", "2024-12-20"), "Sitapur", "Surgical gloves",
         pk["durga2"], c(90, 110, 85), c(431, 433, 436)),
  # The second Kaveri registration supplies Chandgarh
  add_po(c("2024-06-05", "2024-10-14", "2025-01-20"), "Chandgarh", "LED bulb 9W",
         pk["kaveri2"], c(400, 350, 500), c(99, 100, 101)),
  # More regular orders of two vendors
  add_po(c("2024-05-06", "2024-07-22", "2024-09-02", "2024-11-18", "2025-01-27"), "Chandgarh", "Cement bag",
         pk["jaiambe"], c(300, 250, 320, 280, 300), c(380, 380, 380, 355, 355)),
  add_po(c("2024-06-17", "2024-08-26", "2024-11-04", "2025-01-06"), "Madhopur", "Office chair",
         pk["shivshakti"], c(12, 8, 15, 10), c(5450, 5480, 5520, 5560)),
  # Narmada, a large order of paper before the bank change
  add_po("2024-12-23", "Rampur", "A4 paper", pk["bank"], 5200, 262)
)
po <- bind_rows(po, extra) |>
  arrange(po_date) |>
  mutate(po_no = sprintf("PO/24-25/%04d", row_number()), vendor_id = vid(vkey))

# ---- Goods receipts ----
grn <- po |>
  mutate(lag = sample(4:20, n(), TRUE), split = runif(n()) < 0.1 & qty >= 10 & !vkey %in% pv$key) |>
  select(po_no, po_date, qty, lag, split, vkey, office, item)
grn <- bind_rows(
  grn |> filter(!split) |> mutate(challan_date = po_date + lag, qty_received = qty),
  grn |> filter(split) |> mutate(challan_date = po_date + lag, qty_received = round(qty * 0.6)),
  grn |> filter(split) |> mutate(challan_date = po_date + lag + sample(7:15, n(), TRUE),
                                 qty_received = qty - round(qty * 0.6))
) |>
  mutate(grn_date = challan_date + sample(c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2), n(), TRUE))

# ---- Invoices, one per order, raised with the (last) delivery ----
inv <- grn |>
  summarise(qty_received = sum(qty_received), last_challan = max(challan_date),
            last_grn = max(grn_date), .by = po_no) |>
  left_join(select(po, po_no, po_date, vendor_id, vkey, office, item, qty, rate), by = "po_no") |>
  mutate(inv_date = last_challan + sample(0:3, n(), TRUE), inv_qty = qty, inv_rate = rate)

# Planted. Quantity billed above quantity received, cement of Jai Ambe Cement Depot
idx <- which(inv$vkey == pk["jaiambe"])
idx <- idx[round(seq(2, length(idx), length.out = 4))]
short <- c(40, 35, 50, 30)
grn$qty_received[match(inv$po_no[idx], grn$po_no)] <- inv$qty[idx] - short
# Planted. Price billed above the order price, Shiv Shakti Steel Furniture
idx <- which(inv$vkey == pk["shivshakti"])[1:3]
inv$inv_rate[idx] <- round(inv$rate[idx] * c(1.12, 1.15, 1.10), 2)
# Planted. Invoice dated before the order
idx <- sample(which(!inv$vkey %in% pv$key), 4)
early_inv <- inv$po_no[idx]
inv$inv_date[idx] <- inv$po_date[idx] - sample(3:12, 4)
# Planted. Ordered in part, paid in full, the new medical vendor
idx <- which(inv$vkey == pk["newfast"])[c(3, 5)]
grn <- grn |> filter(!(po_no %in% inv$po_no[idx] & duplicated(po_no)))   # keep one receipt
grn$qty_received[match(inv$po_no[idx], grn$po_no)] <- c(1200, 1100)

inv <- inv |>
  mutate(inv_no = paste0(str_sub(str_remove_all(vendors$vendor_name[match(vkey, vendors$key)], "[^A-Z]"), 1, 3),
                         "/", sample(100:999, n(), TRUE)),
         amount = round(inv_qty * inv_rate, 2))

# Planted. Invoices with no order, mostly from Jai Ambe Cement Depot
no_po <- tibble(vkey = pk[c(rep("jaiambe", 4), "kaveri1")], office = c(rep("Chandgarh", 4), "Chandgarh"),
                item = c(rep("Cement bag", 4), "LED bulb 9W"),
                inv_date = as.Date(c("2024-08-19", "2024-11-07", "2025-01-16", "2025-02-27", "2024-10-03")),
                inv_qty = c(300, 280, 320, 260, 150), inv_rate = c(380, 380, 355, 355, 104)) |>
  mutate(vendor_id = vid(vkey), po_no = NA_character_,
         inv_no = paste0(c("JAC", "JAC", "JAC", "JAC", "KE"), "/", sample(100:999, 5)),
         amount = round(inv_qty * inv_rate, 2))
inv <- bind_rows(inv, no_po)

# ---- Payments ----
inv <- inv |>
  mutate(pay_date = pmax(inv_date, coalesce(last_grn, inv_date)) + sample(6:35, n(), TRUE))
# Planted. Paid before the goods were received (chairs of the dormant vendor, and one more)
idx <- c(which(inv$vkey == pk["dormant"])[1:2],
         sample(which(inv$item == "Toner cartridge" & !inv$vkey %in% pv$key & !inv$po_no %in% early_inv), 1))
paid_early <- inv$po_no[idx]
late <- c(12, 15, 9)
grn <- grn |>
  mutate(rowid = row_number())
for (j in seq_along(idx)) {
  r <- grn$rowid[grn$po_no == inv$po_no[idx[j]]]
  inv$pay_date[idx[j]] <- inv$inv_date[idx[j]] + 2
  grn$challan_date[r] <- inv$pay_date[idx[j]] + late[j]
  grn$grn_date[r] <- grn$challan_date[r]
}
# Noise. Receipts entered in the system late, after payment, though goods came on time
idx <- sample(which(!inv$vkey %in% pv$key & !is.na(inv$po_no) & !inv$po_no %in% c(early_inv, paid_early) &
                     inv$pay_date < as.Date("2025-03-15")), 5)
for (j in idx) {
  r <- grn$rowid[grn$po_no == inv$po_no[j]]
  grn$grn_date[r] <- inv$pay_date[j] + sample(3:10, 1)
}
# The new vendor is paid fast
idx <- which(inv$vkey == pk["newfast"])
first_po <- inv$po_no[idx[1]]
grn$challan_date[grn$po_no == first_po] <- as.Date("2024-11-08")
grn$grn_date[grn$po_no == first_po] <- as.Date("2024-11-08")
inv$inv_date[idx[1]] <- as.Date("2024-11-08")
inv$pay_date[idx[1]] <- as.Date("2024-11-11")
inv$pay_date[idx[-1]] <- inv$inv_date[idx[-1]] + sample(3:6, length(idx) - 1, TRUE)
idx <- which(inv$vkey == pk["newok"])[1]
inv$pay_date[idx] <- as.Date("2024-08-17"); inv$inv_date[idx] <- as.Date("2024-08-14")
grn$challan_date[grn$po_no == inv$po_no[idx]] <- as.Date("2024-08-14")
grn$grn_date[grn$po_no == inv$po_no[idx]] <- as.Date("2024-08-14")

# Planted. The Maa Durga variant is paid an invoice already paid to the genuine vendor
dup_src <- inv |> filter(vkey == pk["durga"]) |> slice(2)
dup_row <- dup_src |>
  mutate(vkey = pk["durga2"], vendor_id = vid(pk["durga2"]), po_no = NA_character_,
         pay_date = dup_src$pay_date + 23)
inv <- bind_rows(inv, dup_row)

inv <- inv |>
  arrange(inv_date) |>
  mutate(inv_id = sprintf("INV%05d", row_number()))

# ---- Bank account changes ----
# Genuine changes, made once and kept
gk <- sample(unique(inv$vkey[!inv$vkey %in% pv$key]), 9)
changes <- tibble(vkey = gk, changed_on = sort(sample(work[work > as.Date("2024-05-01")], 9)),
                  new_value = vendors$bank_account[match(gk, vendors$key)],
                  old_value = make_acct(9),
                  changed_by = sample(c("DEO01", "DEO02", "DEO03"), 9, TRUE))
# Planted. Narmada's account changed three days before a large payment, and back nine days after
temp_acct <- make_acct(1)
nar_acct <- vendors$bank_account[vendors$key == pk["bank"]]
big_inv <- which(inv$vkey == pk["bank"] & inv$inv_qty == 5200)
inv$pay_date[big_inv] <- as.Date("2025-01-20")
other_nar <- which(inv$vkey == pk["bank"] & inv$pay_date >= as.Date("2025-01-15") &
                     inv$pay_date <= as.Date("2025-01-31") & seq_len(nrow(inv)) != big_inv)
inv$pay_date[other_nar] <- as.Date("2025-02-03")
changes <- bind_rows(changes,
  tibble(vkey = pk["bank"], changed_on = as.Date(c("2025-01-17", "2025-01-29")),
         new_value = c(temp_acct, nar_acct), old_value = c(nar_acct, temp_acct),
         changed_by = "DEO04")) |>
  mutate(vendor_id = vid(vkey), field = "bank_account") |>
  arrange(changed_on)

pay <- inv |>
  filter(pay_date <= as.Date("2025-03-31")) |>
  arrange(pay_date) |>
  mutate(pay_id = sprintf("PAY%05d", row_number()))
# The account in force on the day of payment
acct_on <- function(k, d) {
  ch <- changes |> filter(vkey == k) |> arrange(changed_on)
  cur <- vendors$bank_account[vendors$key == k]
  if (nrow(ch) == 0) return(cur)
  before <- ch |> filter(changed_on <= d)
  if (nrow(before) == 0) return(ch$old_value[1])
  before$new_value[nrow(before)]
}
pay$paid_to_account <- map2_chr(pay$vkey, pay$pay_date, acct_on)

# ---- Past payments, from the old system ----
past <- vendors |>
  filter(created_on < as.Date("2024-04-01")) |>
  select(key, vendor_id, created_on) |>
  cross_join(tibble(fy = c("2021-22", "2022-23", "2023-24"),
                    fy_end = as.Date(c("2022-03-31", "2023-03-31", "2024-03-31")))) |>
  filter(created_on < fy_end - 60) |>
  mutate(paid = round(rlnorm(n(), log(600000), 1), -2))
active_now <- unique(pay$vkey)
# Vendors with no orders now were mostly dormant before too
past <- past |>
  mutate(paid = if_else(!key %in% active_now & fy != "2021-22" & runif(n()) < 0.8, 0, paid),
         paid = if_else(key == pk["dormant"] & fy != "2021-22", 0, paid))
# Noise. Two dormant vendors who return with small orders
wake <- past |> filter(!key %in% active_now, created_on < as.Date("2021-04-01"),
                      key %in% vendors$key[vendors$trade != "Building"]) |>
  distinct(key) |> slice_sample(n = 2)
past <- past |> mutate(paid = if_else(key %in% wake$key & fy != "2021-22", 0, paid))
past_paid <- past |> filter(paid > 0) |> select(vendor_id, fy, paid)
for (k in wake$key) {
  o <- sample(offices, 1); t <- vendors$trade[vendors$key == k]
  it <- items$item[items$trade == t][1]
  r <- items$base_rate[items$item == it]
  d <- sample(work[work > as.Date("2024-09-01")], 1)
  ponew <- sprintf("PO/24-25/%04d", nrow(po) + 1)
  q <- max(2, round(items$qty_mean[items$item == it] * runif(1, 0.4, 0.9)))
  po <- bind_rows(po, add_po(d, o, it, k, q, round(r * 1.02, 2)) |> mutate(po_no = ponew, vendor_id = vid(k)))
  grn <- bind_rows(grn, tibble(po_no = ponew, challan_date = d + 8, grn_date = d + 8, qty_received = q))
  newinv <- tibble(inv_id = sprintf("INV%05d", nrow(inv) + 1), vendor_id = vid(k), vkey = k, po_no = ponew,
                   office = o, item = it, inv_no = paste0("B/", sample(100:999, 1)), inv_date = d + 9,
                   inv_qty = q, inv_rate = round(r * 1.02, 2), amount = round(q * r * 1.02, 2),
                   pay_date = d + 25)
  inv <- bind_rows(inv, newinv)
  pay <- bind_rows(pay, newinv |> mutate(pay_id = sprintf("PAY%05d", nrow(pay) + 1),
                                         paid_to_account = vendors$bank_account[vendors$key == k]))
}

# Unregistered small vendors, with no GSTIN
paid_tot <- pay |> summarise(total = sum(amount), .by = vkey)
small <- vendors |> filter(!key %in% pv$key) |>
  left_join(paid_tot, by = c("key" = "vkey")) |>
  filter(coalesce(total, 0) < 4e5, trade != "Building") |>
  slice_sample(n = 16)
vendors$gstin[vendors$key %in% small$key] <- NA

# ---- Final tables ----
vendors <- vendors |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, pan, gstin, bank_account, address, created_on)
vendor_changes <- changes |>
  select(vendor_id, field, old_value, new_value, changed_on, changed_by)
employees <- employees |>
  select(emp_id, emp_name, office, designation, pan, bank_account, address)
purchase_orders <- po |>
  arrange(po_no) |>
  select(po_no, po_date, office, vendor_id, item, unit, qty, rate)
receipts <- grn |>
  arrange(challan_date, po_no) |>
  mutate(grn_no = sprintf("GRN%05d", row_number())) |>
  select(grn_no, po_no, challan_date, grn_date, qty_received)
invoices <- inv |>
  arrange(inv_id) |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, inv_no, inv_date, po_no, office, item, inv_qty, inv_rate, amount)
payments <- pay |>
  arrange(pay_date, pay_id) |>
  mutate(pay_id = sprintf("PAY%05d", row_number())) |>
  select(pay_id, inv_id, vendor_id, office, pay_date, amount, paid_to_account)
# The bank's record of payments made from the department's account, by month
bank_totals <- payments |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(pay_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(bank_debits = sum(amount), .by = month)
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("vendors", "vendor_changes", "employees", "purchase_orders", "receipts",
                          "invoices", "payments", "past_paid", "rate_contract", "bank_totals")))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
lakh <- function(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)
crore <- function(x) round(x / 1e7, 2)
inr <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(round(x))
  vapply(s, function(v) {
    n <- nchar(v)
    if (n <= 3) return(v)
    head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(v, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
    paste0(head, ",", substr(v, n - 2, n))
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
vname <- function(id) vendors$vendor_name[match(id, vendors$vendor_id)]
vid_of <- function(name) vendors$vendor_id[vendors$vendor_name == name]
fdate <- function(d) sub("^0", "", format(d, "%d %B %Y"))
```

Let us look at the main tables.

```{r}
glimpse(vendors)
glimpse(purchase_orders)
glimpse(receipts)
glimpse(invoices)
glimpse(payments)
```

The tables are linked by three keys. `vendor_id` links the vendor master to the change log, the invoices and the payments. `po_no` links orders to receipts and invoices. `inv_id` links invoices to payments. Before any test, it helps to draw these links on paper. Every test below is a join along one of them.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, getting the full purchase-to-pay data

Ask for every table of the cycle, for the whole year, in its raw form. That means the vendor master, the purchase orders, the goods receipts with both the challan date and the entry date, the invoices and the payments with the account credited. Most important, ask for the **change log** of the vendor master, sometimes called the audit trail. It shows who changed a bank account, when, from what and to what. The current master alone shows only the last value, and hides a change that was made and then reversed. Ask also for the employee master with bank accounts and addresses, and for earlier years' payments, so that dormant vendors can be seen. Note who ran each extract and when.
:::

## First, is the data complete? {#sec-pay-complete}

A test on incomplete data proves nothing. @sec-jet-complete checked a ledger against the trial balance, and @sec-recon matched a cash book with the bank. Here a quicker check is enough. First, the keys must be unique.

```{r}
c(vendors  = anyDuplicated(vendors$vendor_id),
  orders   = anyDuplicated(purchase_orders$po_no),
  invoices = anyDuplicated(invoices$inv_id),
  payments = anyDuplicated(payments$pay_id))
```

`anyDuplicated()` returns 0 when nothing is repeated. Next, every payment must have an invoice, every invoice a vendor in the master, and every order number on an invoice must exist. `anti_join()` keeps the rows with no partner.

```{r}
c(payments_without_invoice = nrow(anti_join(payments, invoices, by = "inv_id")),
  invoices_without_vendor  = nrow(anti_join(invoices, vendors, by = "vendor_id")),
  unknown_order_numbers    = nrow(anti_join(filter(invoices, !is.na(po_no)), purchase_orders, by = "po_no")))
```

Finally, the payments in our data should add up to the payments in the bank statement, month by month.

```{r}
payments |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(pay_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(our_data = sum(amount), .by = month) |>
  left_join(bank_totals, by = "month") |>
  mutate(difference = round(our_data - bank_debits, 2)) |>
  print(n = 12)
```

Every month agrees, and there are `r big(nrow(payments))` payments worth ₹`r crore(sum(payments$amount))` crore. We can go on. In real work, a difference here is the first thing to settle.

## Vendor master review {#sec-pay-master}

The vendor master decides who can be paid. A fictitious vendor, or a genuine vendor with someone else's bank account, turns every later control into a formality. So we start here. First, a summary of what each vendor was paid in the year.

```{r}
vendor_paid <- payments |>
  summarise(paid = sum(amount), payments = n(), first_paid = min(pay_date),
            largest = max(amount), .by = vendor_id)
```

### New vendors paid at once {#sec-pay-newvendor}

A genuine new vendor is usually registered, then waits for an order, a delivery and a bill. A vendor paid within days of registration skipped some of that, or was created for one payment. Let us find vendors registered during the year and the number of days to their first payment.

```{r}
new_vendors <- vendors |>
  filter(created_on >= as.Date("2024-04-01")) |>
  inner_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(days_to_first = as.numeric(first_paid - created_on)) |>
  arrange(days_to_first)

new_vendors |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, created_on, first_paid, days_to_first, paid)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nf <- new_vendors |> filter(days_to_first <= 7)
trin <- new_vendors |> filter(vendor_name == "Trinetra Medical Agencies")
vin <- new_vendors |> filter(vendor_name == "Vindhya Health Distributors")
dur2 <- new_vendors |> filter(vendor_name == "Maa Durga Medical Agency")
```

`r nrow(new_vendors)` vendors registered in the year have been paid. `r nrow(nf)` of them were paid within a week. Vindhya Health Distributors was paid `r vin$days_to_first` days after registration. Its first order was for paracetamol at Keshavnagar in August, a season of fevers, and it may well have been an urgent purchase. The file will say. Maa Durga Medical Agency was paid `r dur2$days_to_first` days after registration. We meet it again under duplicate vendors. Trinetra Medical Agencies was paid `r trin$days_to_first` days after registration, and ₹`r lakh(trin$paid)` lakh in all, by `r fdate(max(payments$pay_date[payments$vendor_id == trin$vendor_id]))`.

Each test of this section ends by keeping the ids of the flagged vendors in an object whose name starts with `f_`, for flag. We combine them all in @sec-pay-risk.

```{r}
f_new <- new_vendors$vendor_id[new_vendors$days_to_first <= 7]
```

### Dormant vendors that wake up {#sec-pay-dormant}

A vendor that has not been paid for years, and is suddenly paid large amounts, needs a look. Its record may have been reused by someone else. Our `past_paid` table has payments of the three earlier years. A vendor is dormant if it was registered before April 2022 and was paid nothing in 2022-23 or 2023-24.

```{r}
recent <- past_paid |>
  filter(fy %in% c("2022-23", "2023-24")) |>
  distinct(vendor_id)

dormant <- vendors |>
  filter(created_on < as.Date("2022-04-01")) |>
  anti_join(recent, by = "vendor_id") |>
  inner_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  left_join(summarise(past_paid, last_paid_in = max(fy), .by = vendor_id), by = "vendor_id")

dormant |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, last_paid_in, first_paid, payments, paid)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
gomti <- dormant |> filter(vendor_name == "Gomti Furniture House")
others_d <- dormant |> filter(vendor_name != "Gomti Furniture House")
```

`r nrow(dormant)` dormant vendors were paid this year. `r nrow(others_d)` of them received one small payment each, `r paste0("₹", inr(others_d$paid), collapse = " and ")`, which is what a vendor called back for an odd order looks like. Gomti Furniture House is different. Last paid in `r gomti$last_paid_in`, it received ₹`r lakh(gomti$paid)` lakh in `r gomti$payments` payments from `r fdate(gomti$first_paid)`. The size of the return is the signal, not the return itself.

```{r}
f_dormant <- dormant$vendor_id[dormant$paid > 5e5]
```

### Bank details changed around a payment {#sec-pay-bankchange}

A common payables fraud needs no fake vendor at all. Someone changes a genuine vendor's bank account to one they control, waits for a large payment, and changes it back. The vendor complains later that it was not paid, or never notices. The current vendor master shows nothing wrong. Only the change log does. Let us look at it.

```{r}
vendor_changes
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_changes <- nrow(vendor_changes)
```

There are `r n_changes` changes. A change of bank account is normal. Banks merge and firms move. Two patterns are not normal. The first is a change that is **reversed** soon after. We find it by joining the log to itself. A change is reversed if a later change of the same vendor puts back the old account.

```{r}
reversed <- vendor_changes |>
  inner_join(vendor_changes |> select(vendor_id, back_on = changed_on, back_to = new_value, back_by = changed_by),
             by = join_by(vendor_id, old_value == back_to, changed_on < back_on)) |>
  mutate(days_held = as.numeric(back_on - changed_on))

reversed |>
  select(vendor_id, changed_on, back_on, days_held, changed_by, back_by)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nar_id <- vid_of("Narmada Office Solutions")
```

One vendor, `r reversed$vendor_id[1]`, `r vname(reversed$vendor_id[1])`, had its account changed on `r fdate(reversed$changed_on[1])` and changed back `r reversed$days_held[1]` days later. Both changes were made by the same user, `r reversed$changed_by[1]`. The second pattern is a **payment soon after a change**, especially one much larger than the vendor's usual payment. We join each payment to any change of the same vendor in the 15 days before it, and compare the amount with the vendor's median payment.

```{r}
usual <- payments |>
  summarise(usual_payment = median(amount), .by = vendor_id)

after_change <- payments |>
  inner_join(vendor_changes |> mutate(window_end = changed_on + 15) |>
               select(vendor_id, changed_on, window_end, new_value),
             by = join_by(vendor_id, between(pay_date, changed_on, window_end))) |>
  left_join(usual, by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(days_after = as.numeric(pay_date - changed_on),
         times_usual = round(amount / usual_payment, 1))

after_change |>
  select(vendor_id, changed_on, pay_date, days_after, amount, times_usual, paid_to_account)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
big_after <- after_change |> filter(times_usual >= 3)
```

`r nrow(after_change)` payments came within 15 days of a change. `r nrow(after_change) - 1` of them are ordinary payments, no larger than about `r max(after_change$times_usual[after_change$times_usual < 3])` times the vendor's usual amount, into the account then in force. One stands out. On `r fdate(big_after$pay_date[1])`, `r big_after$days_after[1]` days after the change, `r vname(big_after$vendor_id[1])` was paid ₹`r lakh(big_after$amount[1])` lakh, about `r round(big_after$times_usual[1])` times its usual payment, into the account that lasted `r reversed$days_held[1]` days. We follow this case in @sec-pay-case-bank.

```{r}
f_bank <- unique(c(reversed$vendor_id, after_change$vendor_id[after_change$times_usual >= 3]))
```

### Duplicate vendors {#sec-pay-dupvendor}

A PAN belongs to one person or firm, and so does a bank account. Two vendor records with the same PAN, or the same bank account, may be one vendor entered twice. A duplicate record lets the same bill be paid twice, once to each record, and the duplicate checks of @sec-dup, which work within a vendor, will not see it. `filter(n() > 1, .by = )` keeps the groups with more than one row.

```{r}
vendors |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = pan) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, pan, gstin, bank_account, created_on)

vendors |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = bank_account) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, bank_account, address)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dup_pan <- vendors |> filter(n() > 1, .by = pan)
```

Two pairs share a PAN. The two records of Kaveri Electricals also share a bank account, but they have different GSTINs. The thirteenth character of a GSTIN counts the registrations of one PAN in a State, so `1` and `2` mean two genuine registrations, here for two places of business. That is a known and harmless reason. The Maa Durga pair is different. The names differ by one letter, the bank accounts differ, and the second record was registered only in `r format(dup_pan$created_on[dup_pan$vendor_name == "Maa Durga Medical Agency"], "%B %Y")`. A second record with a new bank account is exactly what a duplicate payment needs.

```{r}
f_duppan <- vendors |> filter(n() > 1, .by = pan) |> pull(vendor_id)
```

### Vendors linked to employees {#sec-pay-empvendor}

An employee who owns or controls a vendor has a conflict of interest. The link often shows in the data as a shared bank account, PAN or address. @sec-net-empvendor found such links, including indirect ones, with a network. Here a direct check is enough. We compare each of the three fields, after removing spaces and punctuation and changing to lower case, so that small differences in writing do not hide a match.

```{r}
clean_value <- function(x) str_to_lower(str_remove_all(x, "[^A-Za-z0-9]"))

link_on <- function(field) {
  inner_join(vendors |> transmute(vendor_id, vendor_name, value = clean_value(.data[[field]])),
             employees |> transmute(emp_id, emp_name, office, designation, value = clean_value(.data[[field]])),
             by = "value") |>
    mutate(shared = field)
}

emp_links <- map(c("bank_account", "pan", "address"), link_on) |>
  list_rbind()

emp_links |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, emp_id, emp_name, office, designation, shared)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sag <- emp_links |> filter(vendor_name == "Sagar Lighting House")
sag_paid <- vendor_paid |> filter(vendor_id == sag$vendor_id[1])
```

`.data[[field]]` picks the column whose name is held in `field`, so one function serves all three fields. `map()` runs it for each field and `list_rbind()` stacks the results. One vendor, `r sag$vendor_name[1]`, is paid into the bank account of `r sag$emp_name[1]`, a `r sag$designation[1]` of the `r sag$office[1]` office. It received ₹`r lakh(sag_paid$paid)` lakh in the year. There may be an innocent reason, such as a relative's firm that once used the account. But a vendor paid into an employee's account must be explained, and the employee's role in its orders must be checked.

```{r}
f_emp <- unique(emp_links$vendor_id)
```

::: callout-warning
## Caution, privacy of employee and vendor data

This chapter joins the bank accounts, PANs and addresses of employees with those of vendors. These are personal data. Use them only for the audit, keep them in a protected folder, and do not put full account numbers or PANs in the report. Mask them, or use the vendor and employee ids. @sec-privacy explains how to mask, pseudonymise and store such data safely. A name in a list of flags is not a finding against that person, so share such lists only with those who need them.
:::

### PAN and GSTIN {#sec-pay-ids}

A PAN has a fixed format, and a GSTIN has a check character. @sec-regex-validate and @sec-checkdigits explained both. We reuse the GSTIN check in a compact form. A valid GSTIN must also contain the vendor's own PAN, in characters 3 to 12.

```{r}
gst_chars <- c(0:9, LETTERS)
gstin_valid <- function(x) {
  map_lgl(x, function(g) {
    if (is.na(g) || !str_detect(g, "^[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$")) return(FALSE)
    v <- match(strsplit(str_sub(g, 1, 14), "")[[1]], gst_chars) - 1
    p <- v * rep(c(1, 2), 7)
    total <- sum(p %/% 36 + p %% 36)
    gst_chars[((36 - total %% 36) %% 36) + 1] == str_sub(g, 15, 15)
  })
}

id_check <- vendors |>
  mutate(pan_ok = str_detect(pan, "^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$"),
         gstin_ok = if_else(is.na(gstin), NA, gstin_valid(gstin)),
         gstin_has_pan = str_sub(gstin, 3, 12) == pan)

id_check |>
  filter(!pan_ok | !gstin_ok | !gstin_has_pan) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, pan, gstin, gstin_ok, gstin_has_pan)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bad_id <- id_check |> filter(!pan_ok | !gstin_ok | !gstin_has_pan)
```

Every PAN has the right format. One GSTIN, of `r bad_id$vendor_name[1]`, fails the check, and the PAN inside it does not match the vendor's PAN. They differ in one character. It is probably a typing error in the master. But a wrong GSTIN means that the department's tax records point to the wrong taxpayer, and any tax credit claimed on these bills is at risk. It should be corrected from the vendor's registration certificate, and verified on the GST portal.

```{r}
f_ids <- bad_id$vendor_id
```

### Large payments to vendors with no GSTIN {#sec-pay-nogstin}

A supplier must register under GST once its turnover crosses a limit set by the law. Small local suppliers often have no GSTIN, and that is normal. But a vendor that sells a large amount to one department alone, with no GSTIN, deserves a question. Either it is registered and the master is incomplete, or it is not registered when it may need to be. We do not test the legal limit here, which depends on the kind of supply and the State. We simply list unregistered vendors paid more than a working threshold of ₹10 lakh, chosen by the audit team.

```{r}
no_gstin <- vendors |>
  filter(is.na(gstin)) |>
  left_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  arrange(desc(paid))

no_gstin |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, created_on, payments, paid) |>
  head(5)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nogst_big <- no_gstin |> filter(coalesce(paid, 0) > 10e5)
```

`r nrow(no_gstin)` vendors have no GSTIN. All but one were paid less than ₹`r lakh(no_gstin$paid[2])` lakh each in the year, or nothing. The exception is `r nogst_big$vendor_name[1]`, paid ₹`r lakh(no_gstin$paid[1])` lakh, the same vendor that was paid within a week of registration.

```{r}
f_nogst <- no_gstin$vendor_id[coalesce(no_gstin$paid, 0) > 10e5]
```

## The three-way match {#sec-pay-threeway}

The oldest control in payables is the **three-way match**. Before a bill is paid, three documents must agree. The purchase order says what was ordered and at what rate. The goods receipt says what actually arrived. The invoice says what the vendor is charging. The office should pay for the quantity received, at the rate ordered, and nothing more. Any difference must be explained before payment.

Let us see it on a tiny example of three orders.

```{r}
t_po  <- tribble(~po_no, ~po_date,     ~qty, ~rate,
                 "P1",   "2024-06-01", 100,  50,
                 "P2",   "2024-06-03", 200,  20,
                 "P3",   "2024-06-05", 50,   80)
t_grn <- tribble(~po_no, ~received_on, ~qty_received,
                 "P1",   "2024-06-10", 100,
                 "P2",   "2024-06-12", 150,
                 "P3",   "2024-06-25", 50)
t_inv <- tribble(~inv, ~po_no, ~inv_qty, ~inv_rate, ~paid_on,
                 "B1", "P1",   100,      50,        "2024-06-15",
                 "B2", "P2",   200,      20,        "2024-06-20",
                 "B3", "P3",   50,       90,        "2024-06-18")

t_inv |>
  left_join(t_po, by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(t_grn, by = "po_no") |>
  mutate(billed_over_received = inv_qty > qty_received,
         rate_above_order = inv_rate > rate,
         paid_before_receipt = paid_on < received_on)
```

The dates are text here, but in the form year-month-day, text compares in the right order. Bill B1 matches. Bill B2 charges for 200 units when 150 arrived. Bill B3 charges ₹90 against an order at ₹80, and was paid a week before the goods came. Each test is one comparison after two joins. Now the real data. Some orders arrive in two deliveries, so we first total the receipts of each order. We keep the first and last challan dates and the last date of entry.

```{r}
received <- receipts |>
  summarise(qty_received = sum(qty_received), last_challan = max(challan_date),
            last_grn = max(grn_date), .by = po_no)

paid_inv <- payments |>
  summarise(paid = sum(amount), pay_date = min(pay_date), .by = inv_id)

match3 <- invoices |>
  left_join(select(purchase_orders, po_no, po_date, po_qty = qty, po_rate = rate), by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(received, by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(paid_inv, by = "inv_id")

match3 |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, po_no, po_qty, qty_received, inv_qty, po_rate, inv_rate, pay_date)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_unpaid <- sum(is.na(match3$paid))
```

`match3` has one row for each invoice, with its order, receipts and payment beside it. `r n_unpaid` invoices are not yet paid, and show `NA` in the payment columns. They are the payables at the year end. Now the six tests.

### Invoices with no order {#sec-pay-nopo}

```{r}
no_order <- match3 |>
  filter(is.na(po_no))

no_order |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, office, item, inv_date, inv_qty, amount, pay_date)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
jai_id <- vid_of("Jai Ambe Cement Depot")
n_jai_nopo <- sum(no_order$vendor_id == jai_id)
```

`r nrow(no_order)` invoices were paid with no order. `r n_jai_nopo` are bills of `r vname(jai_id)` for cement at Chandgarh, spread through the year. A bill with no order may be a genuine emergency purchase, approved later. Four from one vendor at one office look like a habit. There is also a bill of Maa Durga Medical Agency, the duplicate vendor, which we meet again in @sec-pay-earlier.

### Invoices dated before the order {#sec-pay-early}

An invoice cannot normally come before the order. When it does, the order was probably raised after the purchase, to regularise it. This is called a **post facto** order.

```{r}
before_order <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_date < po_date) |>
  mutate(days_before = as.numeric(po_date - inv_date))

before_order |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, po_no, po_date, inv_date, days_before, amount)
```

`r nrow(before_order)` invoices, from `r n_distinct(before_order$vendor_id)` vendors, are dated `r min(before_order$days_before)` to `r max(before_order$days_before)` days before their orders. They may be honest regularisations of urgent purchases. They are still a breach of procedure, and worth a line in the report if they are frequent.

### More billed than received {#sec-pay-qty}

```{r}
over_billed <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_qty > qty_received) |>
  mutate(short = inv_qty - qty_received, value_short = short * inv_rate)

over_billed |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_qty, qty_received, inv_qty, short, value_short)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ob_jai <- over_billed |> filter(vendor_id == jai_id)
trin_id <- vid_of("Trinetra Medical Agencies")
ob_trin <- over_billed |> filter(vendor_id == trin_id)
```

`r nrow(over_billed)` invoices charge for more than arrived. `r nrow(ob_jai)` are cement bills of `r vname(jai_id)`, each short by `r min(ob_jai$short)` to `r max(ob_jai$short)` bags. Short deliveries of cement are hard to see at the site and easy to hide. `r nrow(ob_trin)` are bills of `r vname(trin_id)` for surgical gloves, where the whole order was billed but only part arrived.

### Rate billed above the order {#sec-pay-price}

```{r}
rate_above <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_rate > po_rate + 0.005) |>
  mutate(pct_above = round(100 * (inv_rate / po_rate - 1), 1),
         extra = (inv_rate - po_rate) * inv_qty)

rate_above |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_rate, inv_rate, pct_above, extra)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
```

We allow half a paisa for rounding. `r nrow(rate_above)` bills of `r vname(rate_above$vendor_id[1])` charge `r min(rate_above$pct_above)`% to `r max(rate_above$pct_above)`% above the order rate for chairs. The extra is small, ₹`r inr(sum(rate_above$extra))` in all. But the control should have stopped it, and it did not.

### Paid before the goods arrived {#sec-pay-before}

Payment should follow receipt. Here two dates matter. The challan date is when the goods arrived. The GRN date is when the store entered them in the system. Let us flag payments made before the last GRN date, and show both dates.

```{r}
paid_early <- match3 |>
  filter(pay_date < last_grn) |>
  mutate(goods_arrived_after_payment = last_challan > pay_date)

paid_early |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, pay_date, last_challan, last_grn, goods_arrived_after_payment, amount)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pe_real <- paid_early |> filter(goods_arrived_after_payment)
pe_delay <- paid_early |> filter(!goods_arrived_after_payment)
gomti_id <- vid_of("Gomti Furniture House")
```

`r nrow(paid_early)` invoices were paid before the receipt was entered. But in `r nrow(pe_delay)` of them, the challan shows that the goods had arrived before payment. The store simply entered the receipt late. That is a weakness in record keeping, not an advance payment. In the other `r nrow(pe_real)`, the goods arrived after payment, worth ₹`r lakh(sum(pe_real$amount))` lakh. `r sum(pe_real$vendor_id == gomti_id)` of these are the chairs of `r vname(gomti_id)`, the dormant vendor, paid two days after billing and received weeks later.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, a mismatch may be a recording delay

Many breaks in the three-way match are only breaks in the records. A receipt entered late, an invoice keyed in with the wrong date, or an order amended after delivery all look like exceptions. Before treating one as a finding, look at the paper. Here the challan date separated a late entry from a real advance payment. In other data, the store register, the gate entry book or the vendor's delivery note may do the same. If late entries are common, that is itself a point to report, because the system cannot then be relied on to block payment before receipt.
:::

### Paid in full for part of the order {#sec-pay-part}

The tests above look at one document against another. A final check looks at the money. For each invoice, what was paid, and what were the goods actually received worth at the order rate? The difference is the amount paid for nothing.

```{r}
paid_over <- match3 |>
  filter(!is.na(paid)) |>
  mutate(value_received = qty_received * po_rate,
         paid_for_nothing = round(paid - value_received, 2)) |>
  filter(paid_for_nothing > 1)

paid_over |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_qty, qty_received, paid, value_received, paid_for_nothing)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
po_trin <- paid_over |> filter(vendor_id == trin_id)
```

`r nrow(paid_over)` paid invoices exceed the value received, by ₹`r lakh(sum(paid_over$paid_for_nothing))` lakh in all. This one test catches both short delivery and rates above the order. The two gloves orders of `r vname(trin_id)` account for ₹`r lakh(sum(po_trin$paid_for_nothing))` lakh. Each order was received in part but paid in full. Invoices with no order do not appear here, since they have no order rate. They need the test of @sec-pay-nopo.

## Price benchmarking {#sec-pay-bench}

The three-way match checks that the office paid the price it agreed. It cannot tell whether that price was reasonable. For that we compare each purchase with other purchases of the same item. When eight offices buy the same toner cartridge, most of them pay roughly the same. One office paying much more is worth a question.

The fair comparison is with the **median** price of the same item in the same period. The median is not pulled by the few extreme prices we are looking for, as @sec-ano-robustz explained. Let us see the idea on six purchases of one item in one quarter.

```{r}
tiny <- tibble(office = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"),
               rate = c(3400, 3450, 3380, 3520, 4760, 3410))
tiny |>
  mutate(median_rate = median(rate), ratio = round(rate / median_rate, 2))
```

The median is ₹`r median(c(3400, 3450, 3380, 3520, 4760, 3410))`. Office E pays `r round(4760 / median(c(3400, 3450, 3380, 3520, 4760, 3410)), 2)` times the median, about `r round(100 * (4760 / median(c(3400, 3450, 3380, 3520, 4760, 3410)) - 1))`% more. The others are within a few per cent. Now for every order. We compare like with like, the same item in the same quarter of the financial year. `quarter()` with `fiscal_start = 4` numbers the quarters from April.

```{r}
bench <- purchase_orders |>
  mutate(qtr = quarter(po_date, fiscal_start = 4)) |>
  mutate(median_rate = median(rate), orders = n(), .by = c(item, qtr)) |>
  mutate(ratio = rate / median_rate)

bench |>
  summarise(orders = n(), lowest = round(min(ratio), 2), highest = round(max(ratio), 2),
            above_25pct = sum(ratio > 1.25), .by = item)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bsum <- bench |> summarise(highest = max(ratio), .by = item)
max_other <- max(bsum$highest[bsum$item != "Toner cartridge"])
```

For every item except toner, the highest order is at most `r round(100 * (max_other - 1))`% above the median of its quarter. That is the normal spread from transport, quantity and timing. Cement shows no spread at all, since it is bought at the rate contract. @fig-pay-bench shows each order against its median.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pay-bench
#| fig-cap: "Rate of each purchase order as a ratio of the median rate for the same item and quarter. The dashed line is 25% above the median. Only toner cartridges have orders above it."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
bench |>
  ggplot(aes(ratio, item)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, width = 0, alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.25, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Rate as a ratio of the median for the item and quarter", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

Let us list the orders more than 25% above the median, by office, item and vendor.

```{r}
high_price <- bench |>
  filter(ratio > 1.25)

high_price |>
  summarise(orders = n(), median_ratio = round(median(ratio), 2),
            .by = c(office, item, vendor_id))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
hp <- high_price |> summarise(orders = n(), r = median(ratio), .by = c(office, item, vendor_id))
unnati_id <- hp$vendor_id[1]
```

All `r nrow(high_price)` orders are from one office, `r hp$office[1]`, for `r str_to_lower(hp$item[1])`s, from one vendor, `r vname(unnati_id)`. The typical order is `r round(100 * (hp$r[1] - 1))`% above the median.

### The excess paid {#sec-pay-excess}

How much more did the office pay than the median price? For each flagged order, the excess is the difference between its rate and the median, times the quantity.

```{r}
excess <- high_price |>
  mutate(excess = (rate - median_rate) * qty) |>
  summarise(orders = n(), quantity = sum(qty), paid = sum(rate * qty), excess = sum(excess),
            .by = c(office, item, vendor_id))
excess
```

At the median rate, these orders would have cost ₹`r lakh(excess$excess[1])` lakh less. This is an estimate, not a loss. We should say so in those words.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, comparing like with like

A higher price is not always a worse price. Quality differs, as with an original toner cartridge against a compatible one. Small orders cost more per unit. Remote offices pay more for transport. Prices rise during the year, and in a shortage. So compare only the same item, of the same specification, in the same period. Use the median, not the lowest price, as the benchmark. Choose a margin that absorbs the normal spread, here 25%, and write it down before looking at the results. Then ask the office for its reasons before calling any difference excess. The excess is an estimate of what the department could have saved, and it is only as good as the comparison behind it.
:::

## What earlier chapters add {#sec-pay-earlier}

Several tests from earlier chapters apply directly to payables. We run each in a few lines here. The chapters cited explain them in full.

**Duplicate invoices and payments**, @sec-dup and @sec-dup-ssd. We look for the same invoice number and amount under any vendor, and for the same vendor and amount with different invoice numbers.

```{r}
dup_any_vendor <- invoices |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(inv_no, inv_date, amount))
dup_any_vendor |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, inv_no, inv_date, po_no, amount)

ssd <- invoices |>
  filter(n_distinct(inv_no) > 1, .by = c(vendor_id, amount))
ssd |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, inv_no, inv_date, po_no, amount)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dur_pair <- dup_any_vendor
```

The first test finds the same bill, `r dur_pair$inv_no[1]` for ₹`r inr(dur_pair$amount[1])`, under both Maa Durga records. The genuine vendor was paid against an order. The new record was paid again, with no order, after it was registered. The bill is dated `r fdate(dur_pair$inv_date[1])`, before the second record even existed. This is the duplicate payment that a duplicate vendor makes possible. The second test finds pairs of bills of one vendor for the same amount. One pair is `r vname(jai_id)`, where a bill with an order and a later bill with no order are for the same 300 bags and the same amount. The bill with no order may be the same supply billed again. The other pair is two orders of the same quantity a few days apart, with orders and receipts for both, which looks genuine.

```{r}
f_dup <- unique(c(dup_any_vendor$vendor_id, ssd$vendor_id[is.na(ssd$po_no)]))
```

**Bills split below a limit**, @sec-dplyr-split and @sec-nigrini. Suppose that a district office may approve a purchase of up to ₹2.5 lakh, and larger ones go to the Directorate. We count bills between ₹2 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh for each office, vendor, item and month.

```{r}
split_check <- invoices |>
  filter(amount >= 2e5, amount < 2.5e5) |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(inv_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(bills = n(), total = sum(amount), first = min(inv_date), last = max(inv_date),
            .by = c(office, vendor_id, item, month)) |>
  filter(bills >= 3)
split_check
```

`r split_check$office[1]` paid `r split_check$bills[1]` bills of `r vname(split_check$vendor_id[1])` for LED bulbs, all between ₹2 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh, from `r fdate(split_check$first[1])` to `r fdate(split_check$last[1])`. Together they come to ₹`r lakh(split_check$total[1])` lakh, far above the office's limit. This is the vendor that is paid into an employee's account.

**Vendor names spelt differently**, @sec-strsim and @sec-dup-fuzzy. We compare every pair of vendor names with the Jaro-Winkler distance and keep the closest.

```{r}
vendors |>
  inner_join(vendors, by = join_by(vendor_id < vendor_id), suffix = c("_1", "_2")) |>
  mutate(jw = round(stringdist(str_to_lower(vendor_name_1), str_to_lower(vendor_name_2),
                               method = "jw", p = 0.1), 3)) |>
  filter(jw < 0.06) |>
  arrange(jw) |>
  select(vendor_id_1, vendor_name_1, vendor_id_2, vendor_name_2, jw)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
jw_pairs <- vendors |>
  inner_join(vendors, by = join_by(vendor_id < vendor_id), suffix = c("_1", "_2")) |>
  mutate(jw = stringdist(str_to_lower(vendor_name_1), str_to_lower(vendor_name_2), method = "jw", p = 0.1)) |>
  filter(jw < 0.06) |>
  arrange(jw)
jw_other <- jw_pairs |> slice(-(1:2))
```

The two Kaveri records and the two Maa Durga records come first, as the PAN test found. The next pair, `r jw_other$vendor_name_1[1]` and `r jw_other$vendor_name_2[1]`, shares the common words "Medical Agencies", and the two have different PANs and addresses. Name similarity alone is weak. Together with the same PAN or address, it is strong.

**Vendors at the same place**, @sec-geocode-samevendor. We write addresses in one form, removing words like "Shop" and "No." and expanding "Rd", and look for vendors at the same address.

```{r}
norm_addr <- function(x) {
  x |>
    str_to_lower() |>
    str_replace_all("\\brd\\b", "road") |>
    str_remove_all("\\b(shop|no|plot|house)\\b") |>
    str_remove_all("[^a-z0-9]")
}

vendors |>
  mutate(place = norm_addr(address)) |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = place) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, address)
```

The two Maa Durga records turn out to be in the same shop, written two ways.

**The rate in force**, @sec-joins-audit. Cement is bought on a State rate contract, whose rate was lowered from 1 October 2024. A rolling join finds the rate in force on each order date.

```{r}
old_rate <- purchase_orders |>
  filter(item == "Cement bag") |>
  left_join(rate_contract, by = join_by(item, closest(po_date >= effective_from))) |>
  filter(rate != contract_rate)
old_rate |>
  select(po_no, po_date, office, vendor_id, qty, rate, contract_rate)
```

`r nrow(old_rate)` orders of `r paste(unique(old_rate$office), collapse = ", ")` were placed at the old rate after it was lowered, an overpayment of ₹`r inr(sum((old_rate$rate - old_rate$contract_rate) * old_rate$qty))`.

**Other chapters.** The payments in this chapter also appear as journal entries in the ledger. @sec-jet tests those entries for override, such as bills just below an approval limit or entries made at night. The payments must agree with the bank, which @sec-recon reconciles item by item. Large orders should have gone to tender, and @sec-tenderflags checks the tenders themselves. An order split to avoid a tender appears both here and there.

## A risk view of each vendor {#sec-pay-risk}

We now have many flags, each pointing at some vendors. A vendor caught by one test may have a good reason. A vendor caught by several is a better use of the auditor's time. As in @sec-tenderflags-cri, the simplest way to combine them is to count. Each test of the vendor master has already given a set of vendor ids. Let us collect the ids from the other tests in the same way.

```{r}
f_three <- unique(c(no_order$vendor_id, before_order$vendor_id, over_billed$vendor_id,
                    rate_above$vendor_id, pe_real$vendor_id, paid_over$vendor_id))
f_price <- unique(high_price$vendor_id)
f_split <- unique(split_check$vendor_id)
f_oldrate <- unique(old_rate$vendor_id)
```

We put all the sets in one named list, and turn it into one row per vendor and test.

```{r}
flag_lists <- list(
  new_and_paid_fast   = f_new,
  dormant_woke_up     = f_dormant,
  bank_change         = f_bank,
  same_pan            = f_duppan,
  employee_link       = f_emp,
  bad_gstin           = f_ids,
  no_gstin_large      = f_nogst,
  three_way_break     = f_three,
  price_above_median  = f_price,
  duplicate_bill      = f_dup,
  split_bills         = f_split,
  old_contract_rate   = f_oldrate
)

vendor_flags <- tibble(test = names(flag_lists), vendor_id = flag_lists) |>
  unnest(vendor_id) |>
  distinct()

risk <- vendor_flags |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = vendor_id) |>
  left_join(select(vendor_paid, vendor_id, paid), by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(vendor_name = vname(vendor_id), paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

risk |>
  print(n = 12)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_flagged <- nrow(risk)
n_two <- sum(risk$flags >= 2)
```

`tibble()` with a list column, followed by `unnest()`, turns the named list into a long table. `r n_flagged` of `r nrow(vendors)` vendors raise at least one flag, and `r n_two` raise two or more. Those with two or more are nearly all planted cases. Two are not. The genuine Maa Durga Medical Agencies is flagged only because of its twin. One of the Kaveri records shares a PAN for a known reason, and has one bill without an order. Some serious cases raise only one flag. Narmada's bank change and Dhanpur's toner vendor are examples. So the count is a way to order the work, not a filter that decides what to ignore.

A count treats every test as equal. They are not. A bank account shared with an employee is more serious than an invoice dated a few days before its order. @sec-jet-score gave each test a weight. Weights are a judgement. If they are used, the audit team should fix them before looking at the results, and write down the reason for each. It should also check that the ranking does not change much with other sensible weights. The count also ignores money. A vendor with two flags and ₹50 lakh of payments may matter more than one with three flags and ₹50,000.

::: callout-note
## A flag is a lead

None of these tests proves a fraud. Each one says where to look. The work that follows is ordinary audit work. Read the file, see the goods, talk to the people, and confirm with the vendor or the bank. The value of the analysis is that it tests every vendor and every bill, and so points that work at the right places.
:::

## Audit use case, a vendor whose bank account changed before a large payment {#sec-pay-case-bank}

Let us follow `r vname(nar_id)`. First, its whole history in the change log and its payments, side by side.

```{r}
vendor_changes |>
  filter(vendor_id == nar_id) |>
  select(changed_on, old_value, new_value, changed_by)

payments |>
  filter(vendor_id == nar_id, pay_date >= as.Date("2024-12-01")) |>
  left_join(select(invoices, inv_id, inv_no, item, inv_qty, po_no), by = "inv_id") |>
  select(pay_id, pay_date, inv_no, item, inv_qty, amount, paid_to_account)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nar_pay <- payments |> filter(vendor_id == nar_id)
nar_big <- nar_pay |> filter(amount == max(amount))
nar_ch <- vendor_changes |> filter(vendor_id == nar_id)
temp_acct <- nar_ch$new_value[1]
nar_usual <- median(nar_pay$amount)
by_user <- vendor_changes |> count(changed_by)
deo4 <- by_user$n[by_user$changed_by == nar_ch$changed_by[1]]
other_use <- c(sum(vendors$bank_account == temp_acct), sum(employees$bank_account == temp_acct),
               sum(payments$paid_to_account == temp_acct))
nar_po <- purchase_orders |> filter(po_no == invoices$po_no[invoices$inv_id == nar_big$inv_id])
```

The story is clear. The vendor usually receives about ₹`r inr(nar_usual)` a payment. On `r fdate(nar_ch$changed_on[1])` user `r nar_ch$changed_by[1]` changed its account. Three days later, on `r fdate(nar_big$pay_date)`, it was paid ₹`r lakh(nar_big$amount)` lakh for an order of `r big(nar_po$qty)` reams of paper, into the new account. On `r fdate(nar_ch$changed_on[2])` the same user put the old account back. Every other payment, before and after, went to the old account.

Does the temporary account appear anywhere else? We check it against the vendor master, the employee master and all payments.

```{r}
c(in_vendor_master   = sum(vendors$bank_account == temp_acct),
  in_employee_master = sum(employees$bank_account == temp_acct),
  payments_into_it   = sum(payments$paid_to_account == temp_acct))
```

The account belongs to no other vendor or employee in our data, and received only this one payment. User `r nar_ch$changed_by[1]` made `r deo4` changes in the whole year, these two and no others.

The order itself passed the three-way match. The paper was ordered, received and billed at the order rate. So the question is not whether the department owed the money. It is whether the money reached the vendor.

### What the auditor does next

1. Ask the department for the **request behind each change**. A genuine change comes with a letter from the vendor and a cancelled cheque or bank certificate. Check who verified it, and how.
2. **Confirm with the vendor**, directly and not through the office, whether it received ₹`r lakh(nar_big$amount)` lakh in January 2025, and into which account.
3. Ask the bank, through the department, for the **name of the holder** of the temporary account.
4. Find out why `r nar_ch$changed_by[1]` had the right to change bank details, and whether any second person approved the change. A system that lets one user change an account without approval is a control weakness in itself, whatever the outcome of this case.
5. Widen the test. Ask for the change log of earlier years, and for changes of other fields, such as the address or mobile number to which payment advices are sent.

## Audit use case, one office paying more for the same item {#sec-pay-case-price}

Let us look closer at toner cartridges. Is Dhanpur's high price steady through the year, or a passing spike? @fig-pay-toner shows the rate of each toner order by date, with Dhanpur's orders marked.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pay-toner
#| fig-cap: "Rate of each order of toner cartridges in 2024-25. Dhanpur's orders, all from one vendor, are well above those of the other offices throughout the year."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
purchase_orders |>
  filter(item == "Toner cartridge") |>
  mutate(buyer = if_else(office == "Dhanpur", "Dhanpur", "Other offices")) |>
  ggplot(aes(po_date, rate, colour = buyer)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Dhanpur = "firebrick", "Other offices" = "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Order date", y = "Rate per cartridge (₹)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

The gap is steady across the year. Let us compare Dhanpur with the other offices, quarter by quarter, and see which vendors each uses.

```{r}
bench |>
  filter(item == "Toner cartridge") |>
  mutate(buyer = if_else(office == "Dhanpur", "Dhanpur", "Other offices")) |>
  summarise(orders = n(), median_rate = round(median(rate)), vendors = n_distinct(vendor_id),
            .by = c(qtr, buyer)) |>
  arrange(qtr, buyer)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
toner <- purchase_orders |> filter(item == "Toner cartridge")
dh <- toner |> filter(office == "Dhanpur")
oth <- toner |> filter(office != "Dhanpur")
unnati_other <- oth |> filter(vendor_id == unnati_id)
qty_dh <- median(dh$qty); qty_oth <- median(oth$qty)
```

In every quarter, Dhanpur pays about `r round(100 * (median(dh$rate) / median(oth$rate) - 1))`% more than the median of the other offices, and buys from only one vendor. Could the order sizes explain it? The median Dhanpur order is for `r qty_dh` cartridges, against `r qty_oth` elsewhere, so quantity does not explain it. Could distance explain it? For all its other items, Dhanpur's orders sit at the median, with a typical ratio of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(bench$ratio[bench$office == "Dhanpur" & bench$item != "Toner cartridge"]))`, so its transport costs are ordinary. Most telling of all, `r vname(unnati_id)` also sells toner to `r n_distinct(unnati_other$office)` other `r if (n_distinct(unnati_other$office) == 1) "office" else "offices"`, at a median of ₹`r inr(median(unnati_other$rate))` a cartridge. The same vendor charges Dhanpur far more than it charges others.

The estimate of excess is ₹`r lakh(excess$excess[1])` lakh over the year. The total is modest. The pattern is what matters. One office, one vendor, one item, the whole year.

### What the auditor does next

1. Ask the Dhanpur office **how the vendor was chosen** and how the rate was fixed. Was there a quotation, a tender or a rate contract? Were other vendors invited? Link to @sec-tenderflags if there was a tender.
2. Compare the **specification**. If Dhanpur buys original cartridges and others buy compatible ones, the difference may be fair, though the choice itself may then need a reason. Check the printers in use.
3. **Inspect the stock** and the issue register, to see that the cartridges bought were received and used.
4. Check the vendor's other links. Is it linked to any employee of the office, through the tests of @sec-pay-empvendor or a network as in @sec-net-empvendor?
5. Report the excess as an **estimate**, with the method, the benchmark, the margin and the cautions, and invite the department's reply.

## A suggested workflow

1. **Get the full purchase-to-pay data**, including the vendor change log, employee master and earlier years' payments. Record who extracted it and when.
2. **Check completeness.** Unique keys, every payment linked to an invoice and a vendor, and monthly totals agreeing with the bank.
3. **Review the vendor master.** New vendors paid fast, dormant vendors woken up, bank changes near payments and reversed changes, duplicate PANs and bank accounts, links with employees, PAN and GSTIN checks, and large payments to vendors with no GSTIN.
4. **Run the three-way match** on every invoice. No order, invoice before order, more billed than received, rate above the order, payment before receipt, and paid more than the value received.
5. **Separate recording delays from real breaks**, using challan dates or other evidence, before treating any break as an exception.
6. **Benchmark prices** against the median of the same item and period, with a margin fixed in advance. Estimate the excess, and state it as an estimate.
7. **Add the tests of earlier chapters.** Duplicates, split bills, look-alike names, shared addresses and the rate in force.
8. **Combine the flags by vendor**, and rank. Use weights only with written reasons.
9. **Follow up** the top vendors with documents, inspection and confirmation, and record what cleared each flag.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- The vendor master decides who can be paid. Review it, and its change log, before the transactions.
